newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone road blockade lifted.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone road blockade lifted.

text.p: Nigerian-led West African troops lifted a road blockade of Sierra Leone's capital Freetown on Sunday after a first round of peace talks with envoys of its military rulers in Ivory Coast.

But as dozens of food trucks from the provinces rolled into the city, sources close to the force said that Nigerian troops maintained a sea and air blockade as part of efforts to force the reinstatement of civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

The local commander of West Africa troops in Sierra Leone, Brigadier Maxwell Corbie, announced the lifting of the road blockade on a clandestine radio station loyal to Kabbah, who was toppled by soldiers on May 25.

But he coupled this with a tough message, urging civilians to stay away from Sierra Leonean military installations. He said these were potential targets if the junta refused to reinstate Kabbah, who is in exile in neighbouring Guinea..
"I ordered the ECOMOG (West African force) troops holding the Orugu Bridge to withdraw from the bridge and allow vehicles and people to resume using the highway," he said.

"If the talks between ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States) and the military government fail... and ECOMOG is given the mandate by ECOWAS to forcefully remove the coup makers from power ECOMOG will invade Freetown and bomb the city to remove them," he added.
"There will be no escape for the coup makers."
The coup and blockade have tripled food prices.

A delegation from the junta and its rebel allies, who took up arms in 1991 and signed a 1996 peace deal with Kabbah, held talks in Ivory Coast on Thursday and Friday with an ECOWAS committee composed of Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea and Ivory Coast.
They are to meet again next Friday in Ivory Coast, which sponsored the 1996 peace deal.
Sierra Leone's neighbours decided in Guinea on June 26 to pursue dialogue and economic sanctions to try to persuade the junta to reinstate Kabbah, but they retained a military option.

A statement after Friday's talks in the Ivorian commercial capital Abidjan said the two sides agreed to "resolve all issues related to the Sierra Leone crisis peacefully" and would "work towards early restoration of constitutional order".
They also agreed an immediate ceasefire "throughout Sierra Leone". Corbie said the truce seemed to be holding.

Nigerian troops, in Sierra Leone under a pre-coup defence pact, have clashed with junta forces and their rebel allies. So too, have members of a Kamajor traditional hunter militia given extra powers by Kabbah -- much to the regular army's annoyance.
On Sunday, bodies still lay in the streets of Jui, scene of bitter clashes between Nigerian troops and rebel fighters on July 12 and 13, south east of Freetown.
Thousands of civilians fled the fighting. Jui and nearby Hastings were deserted on Sunday. Rebels who held Sierra Leone's second airport at Hastings had also departed.
Nigerian soldiers have clashed with Sierra Leone troops and their rebel allies on several occasions since Nigerian gunboats bombarded the capital in a June 2 show of force.
Kabbah took office in the former British colony in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule.
The rebels rallied to the coup, flooding into the capital Freetown for the first time.
